readingInstruction: Read Psalm 136. You read this on Day 489 as a liturgy of God’s love beside Daniel’s trials. Read it now aloud with a partner if you can, one reading the first line of each verse and the other answering with the refrain. It was probably sung at the temple’s dedication.
settingTheScene: Psalm 136 is the refrain psalm: twenty-six verses, each ending “for his steadfast love endures forever.” It is the refrain sung in 2 Chronicles 5:13, 7:3, and 7:6 at the dedication of the temple, and in Ezra 3:11 when the second temple’s foundation was laid. This week, you have met the refrain at nearly every turn. Today you read the whole song. On Day 489 you read it against exile. Now read it as the temple’s song.
observation: “Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever” (v. 1).
“To him who alone does great wonders, for his steadfast love endures forever” (v. 4).
“To him who by understanding made the heavens” (v. 5).
“To him who spread out the earth above the waters” (v. 6).
“To him who struck down the firstborn of Egypt” (v. 10).
“And brought Israel out from among them” (v. 11).
“It is he who remembered us in our low estate” (v. 23).
“He who gives food to all flesh” (v. 25).
interpretation:
The psalm is a story told in a chorus. The first lines call for thanks to the God of gods and Lord of lords. Then it narrates creation: heavens, earth, sun, moon, and stars. Then it moves to the exodus: striking the firstborn of Egypt, dividing the Red Sea, leading the people through the wilderness. Then the conquest: striking down great kings and giving their land as a heritage. Then the final line: “It is he who remembered us in our low estate.” The psalm covers creation, redemption, and conquest in a pattern of repeated assurance.

The most important feature is the repetition. “His steadfast love endures forever” appears twenty-six times. A modern reader might wonder why. But the people were not reading silently. They were singing, and one group sang the line while another answered. The refrain became a habit of the heart. Hearing it again and again taught them something that could not be taught in one sentence: God’s love does not wear out.

Notice the surprising items in the list of God’s deeds. The striking of Egypt’s firstborn is in the same breath as creation. For Israel, God’s love included his judgment on those who oppressed them. His love is not sentimental. It rescues, and rescue sometimes means defeating the enemy.

Verse 23 is for the exiles: “He remembered us in our low estate.” They knew what “low estate” meant. They had been in Babylon and then returned to a small, ruined city. And God remembered. “And rescued us from our foes.” The last verse reaches out to all creation: “He who gives food to all flesh.” His love covers the whole world.

For the dedication of the temple, no better song could have been chosen. Every item in the list pointed back to the one truth that had held them through everything.
connection: Romans 8:35-39 asks what can separate us from the love of Christ. 1 John 4:10: “In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son.” Lamentations 3:22-23 says the steadfast love of the LORD never ceases. Ephesians 3:17-19 prays that we may know the love of Christ. John 3:16 gives the greatest expression of that love. Psalm 103:11: as high as the heavens are above the earth, so great is his steadfast love.
application:
Read the psalm aloud with someone, and let the refrain sink in.

Write your own “Psalm 136”: a list of ten things God has done for you, each ending with “for his steadfast love endures forever.”

When you struggle with doubt, repeat the refrain.
prayerPrompts: Give thanks to God for his steadfast love, line by line, in your own words.
Thank him for his great wonders.
Thank him for what he has done in your life.
